1:
Ellicott ties the chapter to the one before by an image. In the sixth seal the winds had blown and shaken the fig-tree, and the untimely figs that dropped represented those whose religious life was unequal to the strain of trial. But is all the fruit shaken off? No: those who abode in Christ, purged by their trials, would bring forth fruit that should remain — before the stormy winds had blown they had been sealed with the seal of the living God. The chapter, he says, answers the solemn question with which the last one ended: who is able to stand?

Who the four angels are is disputed. Wesley takes them for evil ones, employed with the first four trumpets, who would willingly have brought on all the calamities that follow but were restrained till the servants of God were sealed. Bede makes them four principal kingdoms — of the Assyrians, Persians, Greeks and Romans . Robertson keeps them angelic and the winds their prisoners, noting that some Jews held the winds from due north, south, east and west favourable, and those from the angles unfavourable.

What the winds are divides them further. Henry makes them errors and corruptions in religion, spirits of error contrary to one another but all doing hurt to the church; and he notes they are called the winds of the earth because they blow only in these lower regions, heaven being always clear of them. From that he draws two things: the spirit of error cannot go forth till God permits it, and the restraint is only for a season, since God first establishes his people and then tries them, having the timing of their trials in his own hand. Clarke and Gill both make the winds historical but date them centuries apart: Clarke to the interval before the destruction of Jerusalem; Gill to the peace after Constantine became sole emperor, when great numbers of the elect were sealed and the winds of heathen persecution blew no more, unless briefly under Julian.

On the angel from the east, Barnes declines to find a meaning. It is not easy to determine what the special significancy is, if any, and perhaps none is to be attached, for it is not necessary to suppose that every minute detail of a symbol receives a fulfilment. Robertson is equally cautious, noting that we are not told why, and reporting the suggestion that Palestine lies east of Patmos. Ellicott takes the quarter as the point: the angel rises into view from the door of the dawn, and in the midst of the dark symptoms of coming storm there springs up a light for the righteous. Wesley makes it symmetrical — the plagues begin in the east, and so does the sealing.

Who the angel is divides the fathers from the moderns. Gill rejects the identification with Constantine and makes him the uncreated angel, the angel of the covenant, the Lord Jesus Christ — for who but he should have the privy seal of heaven, and who could speak so authoritatively to the four angels? Bede reads the east itself as the Lord incarnate, the Angel of the great counsel, bearing the ensign of the cross with which to seal his own in their foreheads. Victorinus alone names a man: Elias the prophet, the precursor of the times of Antichrist, sent for the restoration and establishment of the churches. Clarke keeps it official: the angel is the chancellor of the supreme King. On the seal itself, Ellicott gathers the parallels: the entrusting of a seal to another was the token that royal authority had been delegated, as when Jezebel wrote letters in Ahab’s name and sealed them with his seal. Robertson makes it concrete: the signet ring of an Oriental monarch, giving validity to official documents; and calling God living accents his eternal life as against the ephemeral pagan gods.
3:
The plural in till we have sealed is noticed by two of them. Barnes takes it to mean the angel did not expect to do the work alone, though who were to be associated with him, whether angels or men, is not intimated. Wesley says it flatly: other angels were joined in commission with him. On the sealing Clarke finds a manifest allusion to Ezekiel, and takes it to mean consecrating persons in a more especial manner to God, showing by the mark that they were under his more immediate protection — it being a custom in the east, and in the west too, to stamp with a hot iron the name of the owner upon the forehead of his slave.

Two then look outside the text for a fulfilment. Clarke offers one from history: not one Christian perished in the siege of Jerusalem, all having left the city and escaped to Pella. Gill looks forward: at the blowing of the several trumpets they let loose the winds and let in the Goths, Huns and Vandals, the Saracens and Turks; the retarding was but in appearance, that there might be opportunity to show what care would be taken all along of the church of Christ.

That the seer heard the number rather than saw it is pressed by all three who mention it. Barnes observes that he does not say where he heard it, or from whom, and that the material point is that he heard it and did not see it. Gill turns the fact into a guarantee: he could be sure of the exact number, which did not depend on his sight and counting, in which some mistake might have been made, but was expressed to him.

Whether the number is literal is settled quickly. Barnes gives three reasons for taking it symbolically: the whole scene is symbolical, the winds, the angels and the sealing alike; and it is too exact and artificial to be literal. Robertson adds the arithmetic, that twelve times twelve times a thousand connotes perfection, and that it is not meant to be a complete number even for that generation, let alone for all time. Clarke calls it a certain number put for an uncertain one, since it is not to be supposed that just twelve thousand were converted out of each of the twelve tribes.

Who the sealed are is the real dispute. Ellicott states the literal view and refuses it: some have thought they must be Jewish Christians, taking the twelve tribes literally, but the scope of the previous verses is decisive against it. To limit the answer to Israelitish Christians is to break in abruptly upon the general flow of thought with a bold literalism, whereas the sealed are explained to be the servants of God, and the description that follows proclaims them the Israel of God. Robertson lays out both views and prefers the wider, taking the twelve tribes in a spiritual sense. Wesley holds the narrower: this is not the number of all the Israelites saved from Abraham or Moses to the end of all things, but only of those secured from the plagues then ready to fall — for it seems as if this book had in many places a special view to the people of Israel. Clarke agrees, including in the number all the Jews converted to Christianity.

The list of tribes is odd on any reading, and Robertson says why: it is not geographical, since Levi is included; Dan is omitted and Manasseh put in his place, though Manasseh, as a son of Joseph, is already included in Joseph. He reports the ancient suggestion that Antichrist was expected to come from the tribe of Dan, and that this accounts for the omission. Ellicott raises the same difficulty, asking why there is a change in both the order and the names of the tribes.
5:
Gill treats the roll of tribes as a set of names to be construed, and does it consistently. Judah signifies praise God, and shows that it becomes all the sealed to praise him for all favours, temporal, spiritual and eternal. Asher, which the Septuagint pronounces Aser, signifies blessed, as all the sealed ones are, blessed with grace here and glory hereafter. Simeon signifies hearing, and such a hearing as is attended with obedience, denoting the practical hearing of the Gospel by those who believe and practise what they hear. Zebulun signifies dwelling, and was the tribe in which Christ dwelt and much conversed, denoting his gracious inhabitation among the saints.

Why Judah comes first produces a disagreement. Gill answers that Christ sprang from that tribe, that the pure worship of God was preserved in it, and that it was preserved a distinct tribe until the coming of Shiloh. Wesley says the same shorter: in respect of the kingdom, and of the Messiah sprung therefrom. Barnes denies there is any reason at all — Judah was not the oldest of the sons of Jacob, and there was no settled order in which the tribes were usually mentioned — and proves it by setting three lists beside each other, the order of birth in Genesis, the order in the blessing of Jacob and the order in the blessing of Moses, no two of which agree.

What the list leaves out troubles them more, and Clarke makes three observations. Levi is mentioned, though that tribe had no inheritance in Israel, because they now belonged to the spiritual priesthood. Dan, which did have an inheritance, is omitted, and so is Ephraim. And Joseph is added in the place of Ephraim — Ephraim and Dan, being the principal promoters of idolatry, are left out of the enumeration. Wesley agrees about Ephraim and adds a historical note on Dan that no one else supplies: it was very early reduced to a single family, and that family seems to have been cut off in war before the time of Ezra, for in the Chronicles, where the posterity of the patriarchs is recited, Dan is wholly omitted. On Levi he says only that after the Levitical ceremonies were abolished, Levi was again on a level with his brethren.

Barnes reads the whole roll as a figure. A selection was made as if it had been made from one of the tribes of the children of Israel; but this refers to the Christian church, and means that each portion of the church would furnish a definite part of the whole number sealed and saved. We are not required to understand it of the exact number of twelve thousand, but that the designation would be made from all parts and branches of the church.

He then looks for the fact answering to the figure, and finds it in the survival of the church through the barbarian invasions. Not only was there a suspension of the judgments that seemed to threaten the very extinction of the empire, but there were special acts in favour of the church by which the fierce Northern hordes appeared not merely to be restrained from destroying it, but to be influenced by tenderness and sympathy for it, as if raised up to preserve it when Rome had done all it could to destroy it. It would seem, he says, as if God restrained their rage for the sake of preserving his church, and touched their hearts that they might give Christians opportunity to escape in the impending storm. His instance is the conduct of Alaric, king of the Goths, at the sack of Rome; and he takes the account from Gibbon, whom he introduces with some relish as a writer who will not be suspected of any design to contribute anything to the illustration of the Apocalypse.
9:
Whether this multitude is the sealed company over again is the first question. Ellicott answers that the vision is the climax of the previous one. The sealing represented the Passover of the Church, this vision its Feast of Tabernacles; the sealing assured us that in the midst of severe testing there would be those who would come forth unscathed, and this shows the fruition of their labour and their rest after conflict — the one told us God’s hidden ones would be safe in trouble, the other tells us they have come safe out of it. Clarke and Henry divide them by descent, Clarke making this the Church of Christ among the Gentiles, different from that collected out of the twelve tribes, and Henry saying that the first fruits having led the way, the Gentiles converted later follow.

Where the scene is set divides them. Barnes takes the vision as transferred from earth to heaven, carrying the mind beyond the storms of earth into the period when the church should be triumphant there, so that instead of leaving the impression that the sealed were all who would be saved, the eye is directed to an innumerable host. Gill refuses both the Reformation and heaven: the characters of this multitude and the happiness they enjoy do not suit persons in a state of mortality, and though many understand the vision of the saints in heaven, it rather respects the millennium, the thousand years’ reign of Christ with his saints on earth.

On the robes and palms they agree, varying only in emphasis. Clarke makes the robes emblems of innocence and the palms a token of victory over the world, the devil and the flesh; Henry makes the robes those of justification, holiness and victory, the palms as conquerors used to appear in their triumphs; Wesley calls them tokens of joy and victory. Wesley then turns aside into a digression no one else attempts, on the degrees of reward: there is an inconceivable variety in them, and let not any slothful one say, if I get to heaven at all I will be content — such a one may let heaven go altogether. But who has time to think of this? Who is at all concerned about it?

The cry itself needs guarding, and Barnes guards it. It cannot mean, as the English words would seem to imply, that they desired that God might have salvation: the sense is that their salvation was to be attributed entirely to him. He runs through the word — safety, deliverance, victory, and in the Christian sense admission to eternal life — and notes that one lexicographer renders it here simply victory. Ellicott takes it comprehensively, including every deliverance: from the curse of law, from the power of sin, from the perils of life. Robertson notes it is an accomplished act for those coming out of the great tribulation, and that both God and the Lamb are given the praise.

The staging of the angels is worked out carefully. Barnes places them in the outer circle, outside the elders and the four living creatures, the redeemed occupying the inner circle nearest the throne, and observes that they sympathise with the church triumphant as they did with the church in its conflicts. Wesley sets out the same rings — the living creatures next the throne, the elders round these, the angels round them both — and draws the moral that the heavenly ceremonial has its fixed order. Gill notices what the angels are not: though they have no part in this salvation themselves, they highly approve it as right and just that men should give the glory where it is due. On the doxology, Ellicott counts the clauses: the sevenfold form implies a divine completeness, and is a slight indication that the view which would limit the seals to some short period of Church history is inadequate.
13:
The elder speaks first, and no one is sure who he is. Gill runs through the candidates and dismisses them: not the Apostle Peter, and still less Pope Silvester; more likely Constantine himself, the chief magistrate when the church sprang out of its troubles; or the prophet Isaiah, since many things said by this elder are found in his prophecy — but it is needless to inquire, it is enough that he was one of the four and twenty about the throne. Barnes takes him simply as one of the representatives of the church. Henry reads the question as asked not for the elder’s own information but for John’s instruction, and draws the moral: ministers may learn from the people, especially from aged and experienced Christians, for the lowest saint in heaven knows more than the greatest apostle in the world.

That he ‘answered’ when nothing had been said needs explaining. Clarke calls it a Hebraism for spoke, the question being asked so that the proposer may have the opportunity of answering it; Gill says only that the elder opened his mouth and called to John. Barnes gives it more weight: in Scripture the word often begins a speech, replying to something passing through another’s mind — John was looking on the host and reflecting when the answer came. Ellicott makes it an answer to unspoken longing, and reaches for Dante in Paradise — silent was I, yet desire was painted in my looks. Robertson notes the redundancy is common in the Gospels but occurs only here in this book.

John’s reply is a confession. Robertson takes ‘my lord’ as an address of reverence to a heavenly being rather than an act of worship, and ‘thou knowest’ as at once a confession of ignorance and an appeal for information; Wesley compares Zechariah bespeaking the angel. Henry makes it a lesson: those who would gain knowledge must not be ashamed to own their ignorance, nor to desire instruction from any able to give it.

Who they are divides the readers sharply. Barnes has the eye fixed on a particular part of the host, the martyrs standing among them, and finds a propriety in showing them triumphant while the churches suffered. Wesley flatly denies it: these are not martyrs, for martyrs are not such a multitude as no man can number, but all the souls of the righteous who had lived from the beginning of the world; and the participle is present, taking in those who will come hereafter. Robertson keeps both, saying the martyrs are still arriving from the scene of the great tribulation. Ellicott presses the article — it is the great tribulation — but refuses to limit it to a final crisis, making it what all must encounter who refuse the mark of worldliness on heart, conscience and life. Clarke keeps it plain: persecutions of every kind.

The washing draws the most careful work. Barnes admits an incongruity in making robes white by blood, and reads it by the sanctuary, where things were cleansed from defilement by sprinkled blood. He then presses it into an argument for the atonement: it is not their sufferings that make them white, and if Christ died only as a martyr, what influence could his blood have more than another martyr’s? Such language would be unmeaning. Henry says it shorter — not the blood of the martyrs but of the Lamb; other blood stains. Clarke alone turns it against imputation: the white robes cannot be the righteousness of Christ, for that cannot be washed and made white in his own blood, but are a righteousness wrought in them by the merit of his blood and the power of his Spirit. Ellicott dates the washing by the tense: not ‘have washed’, for it was done during their earthly life; Robertson adds that the result is white, not red, as one might imagine.
15:
The ‘therefore’ is watched closely. Gill will not let it rest on their sufferings: they are there not because of their tribulations but because they were brought through them by the grace and power of God, nor because of their robes but because those were washed in the Lamb’s blood. Barnes says it stronger: no other reason can be given why any one of the human race is in heaven. Ellicott renders it ‘on this account’, and adds that the life is not simply one of joy or safety but one of service.

What the service is divides them. Ellicott notes that those made priests here carry on their service in his temple, but warns this can only be figurative, since in the heavenly city there is no temple. Robertson traces the verb from serving for hire to the ritual worship of priests, and concludes that all the redeemed are priests in the heavenly temple, but that this service is spiritual worship, not external rites. Barnes takes ‘day and night’ as the whole of time: on earth toil is suspended by night, but in heaven, where there is no weariness, there is no need of intermission.

The word for dwelling is the crux. Barnes gives it as to pitch a tent, thinking of the tabernacle in the wilderness. Ellicott says ‘shall dwell among them’ obscures the allusion the seer has in mind: the Shechinah, the glory that rested over the mercy seat, whose restoration in Messiah’s days was a cherished hope of the Jewish doctors. He will tabernacle over them as their pavilion, a shadow from heat and a covert from storm. Robertson marks the preposition: God spreads his tent over them here but tabernacles with them later, both pictures of fellowship. Wesley reads it as his glory spread over them as a covering.

Hunger and thirst go easily; the sun does not. Barnes remembers those who perished of famine and thirsted in pathless deserts; Robertson calls the loss of the two strong appetites a refutation of any gross materialistic conception of the future life; Ellicott adds that the blessed hunger for righteousness is at last appeased, and makes the Eastern sun an emblem of the trials that dry up the springs of strength. Gill takes it both ways: there will be no famine of the word, for though there is no outward ministration of it, the substance will be enjoyed to full satisfaction. Clarke alone reads it historically — the sun not lighting on them means their secular rulers, converted to God, became nursing fathers to the Church, and the heat is persecution, which the Hebrews express by scorching.

On the Lamb they converge. Gill fixes his place: not before the throne like the multitude, nor round about it like the angels, but in the midst, being equal to him that sits upon it. Ellicott makes him the central object in front of the throne, so that whoever would draw near must pass the Lamb. Barnes insists the shepherd’s word means more than feeding: watching, providing, guarding; and reads the living fountains as running streams, not stagnant pools, no image more striking to an Oriental than fountains in burning wastes. Clarke turns them to endless progress: no sameness, no cloying, every moment opening a new source, and since God’s attributes are infinite, through all eternity more will still remain to be opened. Wesley reads the feeding as eternal peace and joy, the fountains as the comforts of the Holy Ghost.

The last clause is Barnes’s. Of the negative descriptions of heaven none is better adapted to console: this is a world of weeping, and philosophers seeking a brief definition of man might have said that he is one who weeps. Ellicott notes that the prophet has tears wiped from all faces while here it is every tear, and that only those who have wept can enjoy the consolation.
